body.heading: Ralph Lauren is Vinted's quiet workhorse
paragraphs: Ralph Lauren doesn't get the hype of Stone Island or Arc'teryx, but it's consistently one of the highest-volume sellers on Vinted. Polos, knitwear, casual shirts and the occasional jacket move constantly, because they're a known name at an accessible price — and because buyers search for them by name.

The flip side of that popularity is a flood of counterfeits. Ralph Lauren is faked at every price point, from obviously bad polo shirts to surprisingly good knitwear. The skill is telling a genuine bargain from a convincing fake — and that's what this guide walks through.
See [what actually sells on Vinted](/guides/what-sells-on-vinted) for the broader data picture; this page focuses on Ralph Lauren specifically.

body.heading: What Ralph Lauren actually sells for on Vinted
paragraphs: Ralph Lauren has a huge price spread, and the average is misleading because it mixes cheap basics with higher-value pieces. The honest picture: polos and t-shirts sell for roughly £5 to £20, casual shirts in the same range, and knitwear — especially lambswool or cotton cable-knit — from around £10 up to £30 or more for good condition.

The value is in the specifics: a plain polo is a commodity, while a well-made cable-knit sweater, a vintage piece, or an unusual colourway holds value better. Condition matters enormously for knitwear, which pills and loses shape with wear.

For the exact current prices, check real sold data rather than asking prices — [see how to see sold prices on Vinted](/guides/how-to-see-sold-prices-on-vinted). It's the difference between pricing to sell and pricing to wait.

body.heading: How to spot a fake Ralph Lauren
paragraphs: 1. **The pony logo.** This is the main tell. On a genuine item the embroidered polo player is crisp and detailed — you can make out the mallet and the rider's leg. On fakes the pony is blobby, misshapen, or overly simplified, and the stitching looks cheap.

2. **The label.** Genuine Ralph Lauren neck labels have clean, evenly stitched lettering. Fakes often have uneven stitching, misspelled sub-labels, or a label that doesn't match the garment's claimed origin or era.
3. **Buttons and finishing.** Genuine polos use good-quality buttons with clean stitching; fakes often have cheap plastic buttons and loose threads. A visibly sloppy hem or seam is a warning sign.
4. **The price.** A 'brand new with tags' Ralph Lauren at a fraction of retail is usually fake. If it seems too good to be true, it almost always is.
For the general fake-spotting framework across all brands, see [how to spot fakes on Vinted](/guides/vinted-scams-buyer-protection).

body.heading: What to buy (and what to skip)
paragraphs: Buy knitwear in good condition — cable-knit and lambswool pieces hold value best and are the most worth an alert. Vintage Ralph Lauren, especially made-in-USA or older labels, has a genuine collector market and can be worth far more than a new polo.

Skip the plain basics unless they're very cheap, because they're commodities with little resale value — a standard navy polo is the same as every other navy polo. The exception is unusual colourways or limited lines, which hold value better.

For the resale angle, read [how to sell on Vinted](/guides/how-to-sell-on-vinted) — the same brand-recognition logic that makes Ralph Lauren sell quickly also makes it a safe category to source for reselling.

body.heading: Why an alert beats refreshing the search
paragraphs: Because Ralph Lauren sells in high volume, the good pieces — a genuine cable-knit in your size at a fair price — go within minutes of being listed. If you're checking manually, you're always behind the people who get notified instantly.

A saved-search alert watches for your exact criteria — brand, size, price cap — and pings you the moment something matching is listed. You still do the pony-logo and label checks before buying, but you're no longer the last person to see the listing.

faq.question: Is Ralph Lauren on Vinted usually real?
faq.answer: A lot of it is genuine, but Ralph Lauren is one of the most counterfeited brands, so check before you buy — look at the embroidered pony logo (crisp and detailed on genuine items, blobby on fakes) and the neck label stitching. Price is a signal too: 'new with tags' at a fraction of retail is usually fake.

faq.question: What is the best Ralph Lauren item to buy on Vinted?
faq.answer: Knitwear in good condition — cable-knit and lambswool pieces hold value best. Vintage Ralph Lauren with older or made-in-USA labels can also be worth far more than a new item. Plain basics like standard polos are commodities with little resale value.

faq.question: How much should I pay for Ralph Lauren on Vinted?
faq.answer: It varies widely — polos and shirts typically sell for £5 to £20, and good knitwear from £10 up to £30 or more. The honest answer depends on the specific item, so check real sold prices rather than asking prices before you decide.

faq.question: How can I spot a fake Ralph Lauren polo?
faq.answer: Check the embroidered pony logo first — on a genuine polo it's crisp and you can make out the rider and mallet, while fakes are blobby and oversimplified. Then check the neck label stitching, the buttons, and the price. A too-good-to-be-true 'new with tags' price is usually a fake.

faq.question: Does Ralph Lauren hold its value on Vinted?
faq.answer: The knitwear and vintage pieces hold value well; the plain polos and t-shirts don't. It's the same pattern as most brands — the specific, higher-quality item holds value, while the commodity basics sell cheap.
